description: Expanded searchable English lesson library for EnglishMaster. Covers core English learning areas from beginner to advanced, but is not literally exhaustive; it can be extended.
usage_note: Search title, category, keywords, explanation, examples, form, and practice. Quiz answer is the zero-based index in options. Lesson content is a curated starter curriculum, not a complete dictionary or every possible English topic.

lessons.title: Simple Present Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the simple present for habits, routines, repeated actions, and general facts. With I/you/we/they, use the base verb. With he/she/it, usually add -s or -es.

examples.note: Add -ies because study ends in consonant + y.

lessons.form: Positive: Subject + base verb (add -s/-es with he, she, it). Negative: Subject + do/does not + base verb. Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?
common_mistakes: She study English. → She studies English.
He doesn't likes tea. → He doesn't like tea.

quiz.why: Use plays with he in the simple present.

lessons.title: Present Continuous Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the present continuous for an action happening now or around the current time.

examples.sentence: They are studying for exams this week.

lessons.form: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. Negative: Subject + am/is/are not + verb-ing. Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?
common_mistakes: She is read. → She is reading.
They are play. → They are playing.

quiz.why: Present continuous needs be + verb-ing.

lessons.title: Simple Past Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the simple past for completed actions at a finished time in the past. Regular verbs often end in -ed; irregular verbs change form.
lessons.form: Positive: Subject + past form. Negative: Subject + did not + base verb. Question: Did + subject + base verb?
common_mistakes: Did you went? → Did you go?
I goed home. → I went home.

quiz.why: After did, use the base verb.

lessons.title: Past Continuous Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a particular time in the past. It often describes the background to another action.

examples.note: An action in progress at a past time.

examples.sentence: I was walking when it started to rain.

lessons.form: Subject + was/were + verb-ing.
common_mistakes: They was waiting. → They were waiting.

quiz.why: Use was with she.

lessons.title: Simple Future Tense
lessons.explanation: Use will for predictions, promises, and quick decisions. Use be going to for plans or predictions based on present evidence.

examples.sentence: Look at those clouds. It is going to rain.

lessons.form: Will: Subject + will + base verb. Going to: Subject + am/is/are going to + base verb.
common_mistakes: She will goes. → She will go.
I going to study. → I am going to study.

quiz.q: Complete: I think our team ___ win.
quiz.why: Will is common for predictions.

lessons.title: Present Perfect Tense
keywords: ever never already yet since for
lessons.explanation: Use the present perfect for past experiences without a specific finished time, or past actions connected to the present.

examples.note: An experience; no specific time is given.

examples.sentence: She has lived here for five years.

lessons.form: Subject + have/has + past participle.
common_mistakes: He have finished. → He has finished.
I have seen him yesterday. → I saw him yesterday.

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: She ___ finished her work.
quiz.why: Use has with she.

lessons.title: Nouns
lessons.explanation: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Nouns can be common or proper, and countable or uncountable.

examples.note: Addis Ababa is a proper noun; city is a common noun.

lessons.form: Countable nouns can be counted (one book, two books). Uncountable nouns are not normally counted individually (water, advice, information).
common_mistakes: an advice → some advice / a piece of advice
informations → information

quiz.why: Happiness names an idea or feeling.

lessons.title: Pronouns
lessons.explanation: A pronoun replaces a noun to avoid repetition. Subject pronouns include I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns include me, you, him, her, it, us, them.

examples.sentence: Marta is kind. She helps people.

lessons.form: Subject: I/he/she/we/they. Object: me/him/her/us/them. Possessive adjectives: my/his/her/our/their.
common_mistakes: Me went home. → I went home.
This is her book; it is hers. → Her comes before a noun; hers stands alone.

quiz.why: Use the subject pronoun he as the subject.

lessons.title: Articles: A, An, and The
lessons.explanation: Use a/an for one nonspecific singular countable noun. Use an before a vowel sound. Use the for a specific or already-known thing.

examples.note: Apple begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.form: a + consonant sound; an + vowel sound; the + specific noun.
common_mistakes: an university → a university (starts with a /y/ sound)
a orange → an orange

quiz.why: Elephant begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: Adjectives
lessons.explanation: An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. It can tell us what something is like, how many, or which one.

examples.sentence: This book is easier than that one.

lessons.form: Short adjectives often use -er/-est; longer adjectives often use more/most. Some are irregular: good, better, best.
common_mistakes: more easier → easier
the most tallest → the tallest

quiz.q: What is the adjective? 'The small cat slept.'
quiz.why: Small describes the cat.

lessons.title: Adverbs
lessons.explanation: Adverbs can describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. They often tell how, when, where, or how often something happens.
lessons.form: Many adverbs are formed with adjective + -ly, but not all: fast, well, often, never.
common_mistakes: She sings good. → She sings well.
He drives careful. → He drives carefully.

quiz.why: Carefully describes how an action is done.

lessons.title: Prepositions of Time and Place
lessons.explanation: Prepositions show relationships such as time, place, direction, and position. For time, use at for exact times, on for days/dates, and in for months, years, and longer periods.

examples.sentence: The keys are on the table.

lessons.form: Time: at 7:00; on Friday; in October/in 2026. Place: at school; on a surface; in a room or city.
common_mistakes: in Monday → on Monday

quiz.why: Use on with days.

lessons.title: Conjunctions
keywords: and but or because although so
lessons.explanation: Conjunctions connect words, phrases, or clauses. And adds information, but shows contrast, or gives a choice, because gives a reason, and so shows a result.

examples.sentence: I was tired, but I finished my work.
She stayed home because she was ill.

lessons.form: Use a conjunction to connect related ideas. Avoid joining two complete sentences with only a comma.
common_mistakes: I was tired, I slept. → I was tired, so I slept.

quiz.q: I stayed inside ___ it was raining.
quiz.why: Because introduces the reason.

lessons.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
lessons.explanation: The verb must agree with its subject. In the simple present, he, she, and it usually take a verb ending in -s or -es; I, you, we, and they use the base form.
lessons.form: Singular subject + singular verb form; plural subject + plural verb form.
common_mistakes: My friends likes music. → My friends like music.
Everyone are ready. → Everyone is ready.

quiz.why: Children is plural, so use play.

lessons.title: Making Questions in English
lessons.explanation: Yes/no questions often begin with an auxiliary verb. Wh-questions begin with words such as who, what, where, when, why, and how.
lessons.form: Simple present: Do/Does + subject + base verb? Simple past: Did + subject + base verb? Be: Am/Is/Are + subject?
common_mistakes: Where you live? → Where do you live?
Does he likes it? → Does he like it?

quiz.why: Use does + subject + base verb.

lessons.title: Active and Passive Voice
lessons.explanation: In active voice, the subject performs the action. In passive voice, the subject receives the action. Passive voice is useful when the action or result matters more than the doer.

examples.sentence: Active: The chef cooked the meal.
Passive: The meal was cooked by the chef.

lessons.form: Passive: subject + suitable form of be + past participle.
common_mistakes: The room cleaned yesterday. → The room was cleaned yesterday.

quiz.q: Choose the passive form: 'They built the bridge.'
quiz.why: Past simple passive uses was/were + past participle.

lessons.title: Reported Speech
lessons.explanation: Reported speech tells what someone said without repeating the exact words. Pronouns and verb tenses may change depending on context.

examples.sentence: Reported: She said that she was tired.
examples.note: Pronoun and tense change in a common backshift pattern.

lessons.form: say + (that) clause; tell + person + (that) clause. When the reporting verb is in the past, present tense often shifts back one step.
common_mistakes: She told that she was tired. → She said that she was tired / She told me that she was tired.

options: He said he is busy yesterday.
He said that he was busy.
quiz.why: A common reported form shifts am to was.

lessons.title: Conditional Sentences
lessons.explanation: Conditionals describe results that depend on a condition. Zero conditional describes general truths; first conditional describes a real possible future; second conditional describes an unreal or unlikely present/future; third conditional describes an unreal past.

examples.sentence: If you heat ice, it melts.
If it rains, we will stay home.
If I had more time, I would read more.

lessons.form: Zero: If + present, present. First: If + present, will + base verb. Second: If + past, would + base verb. Third: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.
common_mistakes: If it will rain, we will stay home. → If it rains, we will stay home.

quiz.q: If I study, I ___ the test.
quiz.why: First conditional uses present in the if-clause and will in the result.

lessons.title: Synonyms and Antonyms
lessons.explanation: Synonyms have similar meanings. Antonyms have opposite meanings. The best choice depends on the sentence and context.
lessons.form: Learn new words with a definition, example sentence, and one related or opposite word.
common_mistakes: Assuming every synonym works in every sentence. Check grammar, tone, and context.

quiz.q: Which word is an antonym of 'early'?
quiz.why: Late is the opposite of early.

lessons.title: Common Phrasal Verbs
lessons.explanation: A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle such as an adverb or preposition. Its meaning may differ from the main verb alone.

examples.sentence: She looks after her little brother.

lessons.form: Learn each phrasal verb as a phrase, including whether it can be separated by an object.
common_mistakes: Using a phrasal verb without checking its meaning or word order.

quiz.why: Find out means discover or learn information.

lessons.title: How to Write a Paragraph
lessons.explanation: A clear paragraph usually focuses on one main idea. It often has a topic sentence, supporting details or examples, and a concluding sentence.

examples.sentence: Reading builds vocabulary and gives us information.
For these reasons, reading is a valuable habit.

lessons.form: Topic sentence → supporting sentences → concluding sentence.
common_mistakes: Changing to an unrelated topic in the middle of a paragraph.

quiz.q: What does a topic sentence do?
quiz.why: The topic sentence tells readers the paragraph's main point.

lessons.title: Basic English Punctuation
keywords: period full stop comma question mark apostrophe
lessons.explanation: Punctuation helps readers understand meaning. Use a full stop for a statement, a question mark for a direct question, commas to separate items or parts of a sentence, and apostrophes for contractions and possession.

examples.sentence: I bought pens, books, and paper.

lessons.form: Start sentences with capital letters and use suitable punctuation at the end.
common_mistakes: Lets eat, Grandma! → Let's eat, Grandma! ('Let's' means let us.)

quiz.q: Which punctuation ends a direct question?
quiz.why: A question mark ends a direct question.

lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.explanation: Greetings help you start a conversation politely. The best greeting depends on the time, relationship, and situation.

examples.note: A polite phrase when meeting someone.

examples.sentence: How are you? I'm fine, thank you.

lessons.form: Greeting → name or introduction → friendly question or response.
common_mistakes: Using very casual greetings in formal situations. Choose language that fits the context.

options: Hello, I'm Dawit. Nice to meet you.
quiz.why: It is a natural and polite introduction.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension Strategies
lessons.explanation: To understand a text, identify the main idea, notice supporting details, use context clues to understand unfamiliar words, and make inferences from evidence.

examples.sentence: A paragraph describes how trees provide shade, fruit, and homes for birds.
examples.note: The main idea may be that trees are useful.

examples.sentence: A character carries an umbrella and wears a raincoat.
examples.note: You can infer that the weather may be rainy.

lessons.form: Preview the title → read for the main idea → find details → check unfamiliar words in context → summarize.
common_mistakes: Choosing an answer that sounds reasonable but is not supported by the text.

options: A guess based on clues and knowledge
quiz.why: An inference uses evidence and reasoning.

lessons.title: How to Learn and Remember Vocabulary
lessons.explanation: Learn vocabulary in context instead of memorizing isolated translations. Review words over several days, make your own sentences, and practise recalling meanings without looking.

examples.sentence: Word: reliable. Example: My friend is reliable because she keeps her promises.

lessons.form: Word → simple definition → example → your own sentence → review later.
common_mistakes: Reading a word many times without testing whether you can remember it.

quiz.q: Which method usually helps you check memory actively?
options: Hide the answer and recall it
quiz.why: Active recall makes you retrieve information from memory.

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.explanation: A verb expresses an action, event, or state. Main verbs include run, think, and know. Auxiliary verbs help form questions, negatives, tenses, and passive structures.

examples.note: Is links the subject to a description.

lessons.form: Identify the verb in a sentence and check its tense and agreement.

quiz.why: Think expresses a mental action.

lessons.title: Modal Verbs: Can, Could, Should, Must
lessons.explanation: Modal verbs express ability, possibility, permission, advice, or obligation. A modal is followed by the base form of a verb.

examples.sentence: You must wear a seat belt.

lessons.form: Subject + modal + base verb. Do not add -s to the main verb after a modal.

quiz.why: Use the base verb after can.

lessons.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
lessons.explanation: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms. Uncountable nouns are not normally counted individually. Use many with countable plurals and much with uncountable nouns, especially in questions and negatives.
lessons.form: many/few + countable plural; much/little + uncountable noun.

quiz.why: Information is normally uncountable.

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
lessons.explanation: Use comparatives to compare two people or things and superlatives to identify the top or bottom of a group.

examples.sentence: A bike is faster than walking.
This is the tallest building here.

lessons.form: Short adjectives often use -er/-est; longer adjectives often use more/most; good → better → best.

quiz.why: Cheaper is the correct comparative.

lessons.title: Relative Clauses
lessons.explanation: Relative clauses add information about a noun. Who is commonly used for people, which for things, that for people or things in many defining clauses, whose for possession, and where for places.

examples.sentence: The girl who won is my sister.
This is the book that I bought.

lessons.form: Noun + relative word + clause.

quiz.why: Who is suitable for a person.

lessons.title: Writing a Short Essay
lessons.explanation: A basic essay has an introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion. The introduction presents the topic and main point; body paragraphs explain reasons with evidence or examples; the conclusion brings the ideas together.

examples.note: Give the reader a clear direction.

lessons.form: Plan → draft → organise paragraphs → revise meaning → proofread grammar and spelling.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a conclusion?
quiz.why: A conclusion wraps up the essay.

lessons.title: Common English Idioms
lessons.explanation: An idiom is an expression whose meaning may not be obvious from the individual words. Learn idioms with their meanings and example situations.

examples.sentence: The test was a piece of cake.
He told a joke to break the ice.
examples.note: He helped people feel more comfortable.

lessons.form: Record the idiom, its meaning, and a natural example sentence.

quiz.why: It means something is very easy.

lessons.title: Polite Requests
lessons.explanation: Polite requests often use could, would, can, and please. Could you and would you are often more polite than direct commands.
lessons.form: Could you + base verb...? / Would you mind + verb-ing...? / May I + base verb...?

quiz.q: Which is the most polite request here?
options: Could I have some water, please?
quiz.why: It uses a polite question and please.

lessons.title: The Verb Be: Am, Is, Are, Was, Were
lessons.explanation: The verb be links a subject to a description, identity, place, or state. Its form changes with the subject and tense.
lessons.form: Present: I am; he/she/it is; you/we/they are. Past: I/he/she/it was; you/we/they were.
common_mistakes: I is ready. → I am ready.

quiz.why: They takes are.

lessons.title: Have and Do as Main and Auxiliary Verbs
lessons.explanation: Have can show possession or experience; do can mean perform an action. Do and have can also help form questions and negatives.
lessons.form: Use do/does in present simple questions and negatives; use did for past simple. After do/does/did, use the base verb.
common_mistakes: Does she likes it? → Does she like it.

quiz.why: After did, use the base form.

lessons.title: Present Perfect Continuous
lessons.explanation: Use the present perfect continuous for an activity that began in the past and continues now, or has recently stopped with a visible result. It emphasizes duration or activity.

examples.sentence: I have been studying for two hours.
examples.note: The activity has continued for two hours.

examples.sentence: She has been running, so she is tired.
examples.note: The recent activity explains the result.

lessons.form: Subject + have/has + been + verb-ing.
common_mistakes: I am studying since morning. → I have been studying since morning.

options: He has been work all day.
He has been working all day.
He have been working all day.
quiz.why: Use has been + verb-ing with he.

lessons.title: Past Perfect Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the past perfect to show that one past action happened before another past time or action when the order needs to be clear.

examples.sentence: The train had left before we arrived.
I had finished my homework when she called.

lessons.form: Subject + had + past participle.
common_mistakes: When I arrived, he has left. → When I arrived, he had left.

quiz.why: Past perfect uses had + past participle.

lessons.title: Past Perfect Continuous
lessons.explanation: Use the past perfect continuous to emphasize how long an activity had been happening before a past point or event.

examples.sentence: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus arrived.

lessons.form: Subject + had been + verb-ing.

quiz.why: Use had been + verb-ing.

lessons.title: Future Continuous Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a particular future time.

examples.sentence: At 8 p.m., I will be studying.
examples.note: The action will be in progress at that time.

lessons.form: Subject + will be + verb-ing.

options: I will be studying at eight.
quiz.why: Future continuous uses will be + verb-ing.

lessons.title: Future Perfect Tense
lessons.explanation: Use the future perfect for an action expected to be completed before a future time or deadline.

examples.sentence: By Friday, I will have finished the project.

lessons.form: Subject + will have + past participle.

options: By noon, I will have finished.
quiz.why: Future perfect uses will have + past participle.

lessons.title: Future Perfect Continuous
lessons.explanation: Use the future perfect continuous to emphasize the duration of an activity up to a future point.

examples.sentence: By June, she will have been working here for ten years.

lessons.form: Subject + will have been + verb-ing.

options: They will have been waiting for two hours.
quiz.why: The form is will have been + verb-ing.

lessons.title: Ways to Talk About the Future
lessons.explanation: English uses several forms for future meaning. Will often expresses predictions or decisions; going to often expresses plans or evidence-based predictions; present continuous can express arrangements; present simple can describe schedules.
lessons.form: Choose the form based on meaning and context, not only on the word 'future'.

quiz.q: Which sentence expresses a personal arrangement?
options: I am meeting my teacher tomorrow.
quiz.why: Present continuous can express an arrangement.

lessons.title: Used To and Be Used To
lessons.explanation: Used to + base verb describes a past habit or state that is no longer true. Be used to + noun or -ing means accustomed to something. Get used to means become accustomed.

examples.sentence: I used to walk to school.
I am used to waking up early.

lessons.form: used to + base verb; be/get used to + noun or verb-ing.

options: I am used to waking early.
quiz.why: Be used to is followed by a noun or -ing.

lessons.title: Gerunds and Infinitives
lessons.explanation: A gerund is an -ing form used like a noun. An infinitive is commonly to + base verb. Some verbs take one form, some the other, and some allow both with a change in meaning.

examples.note: Enjoy is followed by a gerund.
Want is followed by an infinitive.

lessons.form: Learn common patterns: enjoy + -ing; want/hope/plan + to-infinitive.
lessons.common_mistakes: I enjoy to read. → I enjoy reading.

quiz.why: Decide is commonly followed by to + verb.

lessons.title: Bare Infinitives
lessons.explanation: A bare infinitive is the base form without 'to'. It follows modal verbs and certain verbs such as let and make in active structures.
lessons.form: Modal + base verb; let/make + object + base verb in common active patterns.

quiz.why: Use the base verb after can.

lessons.title: Determiners: This, That, Some, Any, Each, Every
lessons.explanation: Determiners come before nouns and help identify or quantify them. This/that indicate distance, some/any refer to an unspecified amount or number, and each/every focus on members of a group.

examples.note: These goes with plural nouns nearby.
Every is followed by a singular noun and verb.

lessons.form: Determiner + noun; check number, meaning, and sentence type.

quiz.why: Every is followed by a singular noun.

lessons.title: Quantifiers: Some, Any, Much, Many, Few, Little
lessons.explanation: Quantifiers show amount or number. Many and few are used with countable plural nouns; much and little are used with uncountable nouns. Some and any work with both, depending on context.
lessons.form: many/few + countable plural; much/little + uncountable; a lot of + either.

quiz.why: Chairs are countable.

lessons.title: Some and Any
lessons.explanation: Some is common in positive statements and offers or requests expecting a yes. Any is common in negatives and many questions, but usage depends on meaning.
lessons.form: Choose some or any based on sentence type and intended meaning.

options: Would you like a tea water?
quiz.why: Some is common in offers.

lessons.title: Subject and Object
lessons.explanation: The subject tells who or what the sentence is about and often performs the action. The object receives the action or is affected by it.

examples.note: Mimi is subject; door is object.
Us is an indirect object; homework is a direct object.

lessons.form: Subject + verb + (object), depending on the verb.

quiz.q: In 'The boy kicked the ball,' what is the object?
quiz.why: The ball receives the action.

lessons.title: Types of Sentences
lessons.explanation: The four common sentence types are declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request), and exclamatory (strong feeling).
lessons.form: Identify the purpose and punctuation of each sentence.

quiz.why: It gives a polite instruction.

lessons.title: Sentence Fragments and Run-on Sentences
lessons.explanation: A fragment is an incomplete sentence presented as a full one. A run-on joins independent clauses incorrectly. Fix them by completing the idea or using punctuation and conjunctions correctly.

examples.sentence: I was late, so I hurried.

lessons.form: Use a full stop, semicolon where appropriate, or comma + coordinating conjunction to join independent clauses.

options: The bus was late, so I walked.
quiz.why: It expresses a complete thought and joins clauses correctly.

lessons.title: Capitalization Rules
lessons.explanation: Use capital letters at the start of sentences, for the pronoun I, proper nouns, names of countries and languages, and days and months.

examples.note: I, English, and Monday are capitalized.

lessons.form: Capitalize sentence beginnings and proper nouns.
lessons.common_mistakes: i live in ethiopia. → I live in Ethiopia.

quiz.why: I and English need capitals.

lessons.title: Apostrophes: Contractions and Possession
lessons.explanation: Apostrophes show omitted letters in contractions and possession. Its is possessive; it's means it is or it has. Their is possessive; they're means they are.

examples.note: They're = they are; their shows possession.

lessons.form: Check whether the word means a contraction or possession.
lessons.common_mistakes: Its a good day. → It's a good day.

quiz.why: Its is possessive.

lessons.title: Using Commas
lessons.explanation: Commas separate items in a list, set off some introductory elements, mark direct address, and help join independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction.

examples.sentence: I bought rice, beans, and fruit.

lessons.form: Use commas to make structure clear, not simply wherever you pause.

options: I was tired, so I slept.
I was tired so, I slept.
I, was tired so I slept.
quiz.why: Use a comma before so joining independent clauses.

lessons.title: Semicolons and Colons
lessons.explanation: A semicolon can join closely related independent clauses. A colon can introduce an explanation, example, or list after a complete clause.

examples.sentence: The road was closed; we took another route.
Bring three things: a pen, paper, and a book.

lessons.form: Use a semicolon between related independent clauses; use a colon after a complete introductory clause.

options: A list after a complete clause
quiz.why: A colon often introduces a list or explanation.

lessons.title: Relative Pronouns and Clauses
lessons.explanation: Relative pronouns connect information to a noun. Who is a subject form for people; whom is an object form in formal English; whose shows possession; which is used for things; that is common in defining clauses.

examples.sentence: The person who called is here.
The person whom I met was kind.

lessons.form: Choose a relative pronoun that fits the role and style.

quiz.why: Whose expresses possession.

lessons.title: Linking Words and Transitions
lessons.explanation: Linking words show relationships between ideas: addition, contrast, cause, result, sequence, or example. Choose one that matches the logic and punctuate it correctly.

examples.sentence: It was raining; however, we continued.
The road was closed; therefore, we took another route.

lessons.form: Choose transitions by meaning; punctuation depends on where they appear.

quiz.why: However signals contrast.

lessons.title: Paraphrasing and Summarizing
lessons.explanation: Paraphrasing restates a specific idea in new wording and structure while preserving meaning. Summarizing gives only the main points in a shorter form. When using a source, credit it as required.

examples.sentence: Original: The road was blocked by heavy snow.
examples.note: Paraphrase: Heavy snowfall made the road impassable.

lessons.form: Understand the source first, write from memory, compare meaning, and acknowledge sources when needed.

quiz.why: A summary condenses the main ideas.

lessons.title: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.explanation: Prefixes are added to the beginning of a word and suffixes to the end. They can change meaning or word class.
lessons.form: Learn common affixes and notice spelling changes.

quiz.q: What does the prefix 're-' often mean?
quiz.why: Re- often means again.

lessons.title: Collocations: Natural Word Partnerships
lessons.explanation: Collocations are words that commonly occur together. Learning them helps speech and writing sound natural.
lessons.form: Learn vocabulary in phrases, not only as isolated words.

quiz.why: Do homework is the standard collocation.

lessons.title: Commonly Confused Words
lessons.explanation: Some English words sound alike or look similar but have different meanings. Use grammar and context to choose the correct form.
lessons.form: Replace contractions with their full forms to check meaning.

quiz.why: They're means they are.

lessons.title: Common Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.explanation: A prefix changes a word at the beginning; a suffix changes it at the end. The effect depends on the word and affix.
lessons.form: Use a dictionary to confirm how an affix changes meaning and grammar.

quiz.why: Hopeless means without hope.

lessons.title: Parts of Speech
lessons.explanation: Words are grouped by the jobs they do in a sentence. Main categories include nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections.

examples.sentence: The very small bird sang beautifully.
examples.note: Bird is noun; small is adjective; beautifully is adverb.

lessons.form: Classify a word by its role in context; one word can belong to different classes in different sentences.

quiz.why: Beautifully modifies the verb sings.

lessons.title: Formal and Informal English
lessons.explanation: English changes according to audience and situation. Formal English is often used in academic or professional writing; informal English is common with friends and casual conversation.

examples.sentence: Formal: I would appreciate your assistance.
Informal: Can you give me a hand?

lessons.form: Choose vocabulary and contractions appropriate to the audience and purpose.

quiz.q: Which is most suitable for a formal email?
options: Could you please send the document?
quiz.why: It is polite and professional.

lessons.title: Small Talk and Keeping a Conversation Going
lessons.explanation: Small talk is brief friendly conversation about shared or everyday topics. Open questions and follow-up questions help keep it going.
lessons.form: Ask, listen, respond to what was said, and ask a related follow-up question.

quiz.q: Which question best invites a longer answer?
options: What do you enjoy doing in your free time?
quiz.why: It invites details.

lessons.title: Giving Opinions and Agreeing Politely
lessons.explanation: Use phrases such as 'I think', 'In my opinion', 'I agree because', and 'I see your point, but...' to share ideas respectfully.

examples.sentence: In my opinion, public libraries are important.
I see your point, but I have a different view.

lessons.form: State the opinion, give a reason or example, and respond respectfully.

quiz.why: It acknowledges the other person's view.

lessons.title: Telephone and Video Call English
lessons.explanation: Phone calls often need clear openings, introductions, requests, clarification, and polite endings.
lessons.form: Greeting → identify yourself → explain purpose → clarify → close politely.

quiz.q: What can you say when you did not hear?
quiz.why: It is a polite clarification request.

lessons.title: Job and School Interview English
lessons.explanation: Interview answers should be relevant, truthful, and supported by examples. Prepare a concise introduction, strengths, experiences, and questions for the interviewer.

examples.sentence: One strength of mine is teamwork. For example...
examples.note: A claim supported by an example.

lessons.form: Answer directly, give a specific example, and connect it to the role or task.

quiz.q: A strong interview answer should be:
options: Relevant and supported by an example
quiz.why: Specific truthful examples are stronger.

lessons.title: Writing Clear Emails
lessons.explanation: A clear email has a useful subject, greeting, purpose, necessary details, and suitable closing. Formality depends on the recipient.

examples.sentence: Dear Ms. Bekele, ... Kind regards, Hana

lessons.form: Subject → greeting → purpose → details/action requested → closing → name.

quiz.q: What helps the reader understand an email quickly?
quiz.why: A clear subject previews the message.

lessons.title: Formal and Informal Letters
lessons.explanation: Letters vary by purpose. Formal letters use respectful language and clear paragraphs; informal letters can be more personal and conversational.

examples.note: Formal salutation when the recipient is unknown.
Informal greeting to someone you know.

lessons.form: Greeting → reason for writing → details → requested action or closing.

quiz.why: It is a conventional formal greeting.

lessons.title: Writing a Short Story
lessons.explanation: A short story often includes characters, setting, a problem or conflict, events that develop it, and an ending. Use specific details and consistent tense.

examples.sentence: At sunset, a student found a locked box.

lessons.form: Plan character + setting + problem + key events + resolution.

quiz.q: What usually drives a story forward?
quiz.why: A problem gives the events direction.

lessons.title: Descriptive Writing
lessons.explanation: Descriptive writing helps readers imagine a person, place, object, or experience. Use precise nouns, strong verbs, and relevant sensory details without overloading every sentence with adjectives.

examples.sentence: Warm bread filled the small kitchen with a sweet smell.

lessons.form: Choose a focus → observe details → organise by space or importance → revise for precision.

quiz.why: Specific details help readers picture the scene.

lessons.title: Using Context Clues
lessons.explanation: Context clues are nearby words or ideas that help you infer an unfamiliar word's meaning. Clues may include examples, contrast, explanation, or cause and effect.

examples.sentence: Unlike his timid brother, Amir was bold.
examples.note: Unlike signals contrast; bold is opposite to timid.

lessons.form: Read the whole sentence and paragraph, predict a meaning, then verify it.

quiz.q: What can help you infer an unfamiliar word?
options: Guessing only from the first letter
quiz.why: Context supplies clues.

lessons.title: Main Idea and Supporting Details
lessons.explanation: The main idea is the central point of a text or paragraph. Supporting details explain, illustrate, or provide evidence for it.

examples.sentence: A paragraph lists exercise benefits: stronger muscles, better sleep, and improved mood.
examples.note: The main idea may be that exercise has several benefits.

lessons.form: Ask: What is this mostly about? Which details support that point?

options: Explain or support the main idea
quiz.why: They develop the main point.

lessons.title: Making Inferences
lessons.explanation: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues in a text plus what you already know. A good inference is supported by evidence rather than pure imagination.

examples.sentence: The ground is wet and people carry umbrellas.

lessons.form: Find a clue → combine it with reasonable background knowledge → state a cautious conclusion.

quiz.q: An inference should be based on:
quiz.why: Evidence supports a reasonable conclusion.

lessons.title: Listening and Note-Taking Strategies
lessons.explanation: Effective listening begins with a purpose. Listen first for the general idea, then for key details. Write keywords rather than every word and review notes soon afterward.

examples.sentence: Lecture topic: causes of pollution; notes: vehicles, factories, waste.

lessons.form: Before listening: predict topic. During: note main points. After: organise and check gaps.

quiz.why: Notes should capture important information.

lessons.title: Word Stress
lessons.explanation: In English, one syllable in many words is more prominent. Stress can help listeners identify words and sometimes distinguish meanings or word classes.

examples.note: Stress changes by word class in this example.

lessons.form: Listen to a reliable pronunciation model, mark the stressed syllable, and practise aloud.

quiz.why: Stress makes one syllable more prominent.

lessons.title: Sentence Stress and Rhythm
lessons.explanation: English speech often stresses important content words and reduces many grammatical function words. Stress can change which information sounds most important.

examples.note: Blue is emphasized to contrast colour.

lessons.form: Practise short phrases, stress key words, and listen for reductions in natural speech.

quiz.why: Stress highlights important information.

lessons.title: Pronouncing the TH Sounds
lessons.explanation: English has two common 'th' sounds: the unvoiced sound in think and the voiced sound in this. Tongue placement near the teeth helps produce both.
lessons.form: Place the tongue lightly near or between the teeth and practise slowly, then in sentences.

quiz.q: Which word usually has voiced th?
quiz.why: This begins with voiced th.

lessons.title: English Vowel Sounds
lessons.explanation: English spelling does not always predict vowel pronunciation. Small vowel differences can distinguish words, so listening and repeated practice are useful.

examples.note: Short and long vowel contrast for many accents.

lessons.form: Use audio from a trusted dictionary and practise minimal pairs in context.

quiz.q: Why can pronunciation be hard to predict from spelling?
options: Letters and sounds do not always match one-to-one
quiz.why: Spelling-sound patterns are not perfectly consistent.

lessons.title: Numbers, Dates, and Time
lessons.explanation: Learn cardinal numbers (one, two), ordinal numbers (first, second), dates, years, and common ways to tell the time. Spoken date formats vary by region.
lessons.form: Practise both saying and writing times and dates; follow the format expected in your context.

quiz.why: Ordinal numbers show order.

lessons.title: Shopping and Money Vocabulary
lessons.explanation: Useful shopping language includes asking prices, sizes, availability, payment methods, and receipts. Check whether prices are per item or per unit.

examples.sentence: Could I try this in a larger size?

lessons.form: Polite question + item or service + specific detail.

quiz.q: Which phrase asks for a price?
quiz.why: It asks the cost.

lessons.title: Travel and Directions
lessons.explanation: Travel vocabulary helps you ask for directions, understand transport information, and describe locations. Direction phrases include turn left, go straight, and next to.

examples.sentence: Go straight and turn right at the bank.
Is there a bus stop nearby?

lessons.form: Ask politely, listen for landmarks, and confirm important directions.

quiz.why: It gives a direction.

lessons.title: Health and Everyday Wellbeing Vocabulary
lessons.explanation: Learn common phrases for describing symptoms and asking for help. For serious or urgent health concerns, communicate clearly with a qualified professional.

examples.sentence: I'd like to make an appointment.

lessons.form: Symptom + duration + severity + request for help, when relevant.

quiz.why: A sore throat is a symptom.

lessons.title: School and Workplace Vocabulary
lessons.explanation: School and workplace vocabulary includes assignments, deadlines, meetings, schedules, feedback, colleagues, and responsibilities.

examples.sentence: The assignment is due on Friday.

lessons.form: Learn the word, its common partners, and one situation where it is used.

options: The time something must be finished by
quiz.why: A deadline is the completion time limit.

lessons.title: Active Recall and Spaced Review
lessons.explanation: Active recall means trying to remember information without looking at the answer. Spaced review means revisiting material at increasing intervals. Both can help learning when used consistently.

examples.sentence: Close your notes and explain the tense from memory.
Review a word tomorrow and again several days later.

lessons.form: Study → recall without notes → check errors → review later.

options: Trying to retrieve information from memory
quiz.why: It requires retrieving information.

lessons.title: Common Irregular Verbs
lessons.explanation: Irregular verbs do not form the past simply by adding -ed. Learn their base, past simple, and past participle forms together.
lessons.form: Base form / past simple / past participle. Use the past participle with have/has/had and in many passive structures.

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Yesterday, I ___ a bird.'
quiz.why: Simple past of see is saw.

lessons.title: Regular Verb Spelling in the Past
lessons.explanation: Most regular verbs form the past with -ed, but spelling and pronunciation vary. Some verbs add -d, change y to i, or double a final consonant under common patterns.
lessons.form: Check the ending and syllable/stress pattern; there are exceptions.

quiz.why: Consonant + y commonly changes to -ied.

lessons.title: Making Negative Sentences
lessons.explanation: Negatives often use not after an auxiliary verb. When there is no auxiliary in the simple present or past, use do/does/did + not + base verb.

examples.sentence: They do not play on Sundays.

lessons.form: Be/modal + not; otherwise use do/does/did + not + base verb.

quiz.why: Doesn't is followed by the base verb.

lessons.title: Question Tags
lessons.explanation: Question tags are short questions added to statements. A positive statement often takes a negative tag, and a negative statement often takes a positive tag. The auxiliary and pronoun must match.
lessons.form: Statement + matching auxiliary + pronoun; intonation can show whether a real answer is expected.

quiz.why: The tag matches you and the positive statement.

lessons.title: Indirect Questions
lessons.explanation: Indirect questions are more polite or less direct. After an opening phrase such as 'Could you tell me', use statement word order rather than question word order.

examples.sentence: Indirect: Could you tell me where the station is?
examples.note: Statement word order inside the indirect question.

lessons.form: Opening phrase + question word + subject + verb.

options: Could you tell me where is the bank?
Could you tell me where the bank is?
Could you tell where the bank?
quiz.why: Use subject + verb order in the embedded question.

lessons.title: Common Preposition Patterns
lessons.explanation: Many adjectives and verbs commonly pair with particular prepositions. These combinations often need to be learned as whole phrases.
lessons.form: Record the full phrase and an example sentence; usage can vary by meaning.

quiz.why: Interested is commonly followed by in.

lessons.title: Quotation Marks and Dialogue
lessons.explanation: Quotation marks mark direct speech in many English writing styles. Punctuation conventions vary between American and British styles, so be consistent with the style you choose.

examples.note: Direct speech in a common style.

lessons.form: Introduce speech clearly and keep punctuation style consistent.

quiz.q: Quotation marks are often used to show:
quiz.why: They mark exact words in direct speech.

lessons.title: Editing and Proofreading
lessons.explanation: Revision improves ideas and organisation; editing improves clarity and sentence structure; proofreading checks surface errors such as spelling, punctuation, and typos.

examples.sentence: First check the main argument, then grammar and spelling.

lessons.form: Revise ideas → edit sentences → proofread mechanics; read aloud to catch awkward phrasing.

options: New research unrelated to the draft
quiz.why: Proofreading checks surface errors.

lessons.title: Writing a Simple CV or Résumé
lessons.explanation: A CV or résumé presents relevant education, skills, experience, and achievements clearly and honestly. Use consistent formatting and action verbs, and tailor details to the opportunity.

examples.sentence: Organised a school club event for 30 students.

lessons.form: Contact details → profile if useful → education → relevant experience/skills → achievements.

quiz.why: Accuracy and relevance build credibility.

lessons.title: Skimming and Scanning
lessons.explanation: Skimming means reading quickly to understand the general idea. Scanning means searching for a particular fact, number, name, or keyword.

examples.sentence: Read the headings to get the topic.
Find the date in a timetable.

lessons.form: Choose skimming for gist and scanning for a specific detail.

quiz.q: To find a phone number quickly, use:
quiz.why: Scanning searches for a specific detail.

lessons.title: Listening for Gist and Detail
lessons.explanation: Listening for gist means identifying the overall message. Listening for detail means focusing on specific facts, names, times, or reasons.

examples.sentence: First listen: What is the conversation about?
Second listen: What time is the meeting?

lessons.form: Listen once for the topic and again for the details if possible.

quiz.q: Listening for gist means listening for:
quiz.why: Gist is the overall meaning.

lessons.title: Asking for Clarification
lessons.explanation: When you do not understand, ask politely for repetition, slower speech, an example, or clarification.

examples.sentence: Could you speak a little more slowly?
What do you mean by this word?

lessons.form: Could you repeat/explain...? / What does ... mean? / Do you mean ...?

quiz.q: Which phrase asks someone to repeat?
options: Could you say that again, please?
quiz.why: It directly and politely asks for repetition.

lessons.title: Giving a Short Presentation
lessons.explanation: A clear presentation has an opening, a small number of organised points, signposting phrases, examples, and a conclusion. Practise aloud and use notes rather than reading every word.

examples.sentence: Today, I'll talk about three benefits of reading.

lessons.form: Opening → point 1 → point 2 → point 3 → summary → questions.

quiz.q: What helps listeners follow a presentation?
quiz.why: Signposting helps the audience follow ideas.

lessons.title: Apologies and Responding Politely
lessons.explanation: Use 'I'm sorry' to apologise, explain briefly when useful, and offer to correct a problem. Responses depend on seriousness and context.

examples.sentence: That's okay. Thanks for telling me.

lessons.form: Acknowledge the problem → apologise → explain or repair if appropriate.

options: I am sorry I interrupted you.
You must be happy I broke it.
quiz.why: It clearly apologises for an action.

lessons.title: Using Dictionaries and Reliable Sources
lessons.explanation: A learner's dictionary can provide definitions, pronunciation audio, word class, example sentences, and usage labels. Compare sources when a phrase is unfamiliar and consider context and regional variation.

examples.sentence: Check whether a word is a noun or verb.
examples.note: Word class helps you use it correctly.

lessons.form: Look up meaning → listen to pronunciation → read examples → write your own sentence.

quiz.q: A learner's dictionary can help with:
quiz.why: Dictionaries support meaning and pronunciation.
